#6511. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear," author and environmental historian Peter S. Alagona looks at the models used to develop the U.S. grizzly bear recovery program, and how California could make an ideal home for a new population.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are.

But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet" (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out.

Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. They assume that conservation efforts should focus on the best remaining grizzly habitats, and that we can best understand those habitats by studying bears in the places where they still live.

The result has, indeed, been a far better understanding of grizzly habitat use. But this approach has also produced a circular logic with a structural bias toward the status quo. In most grizzly habitat models, past realities and future possibilities fade. With each new study, it seems more and more like the only possible places for grizzlies are the exact kinds of places where they currently live.

The six recovery areas identified in the 1993 Recovery Plan were all places where grizzlies still lived or had recently lived when they were listed as threatened in 1975. The plan argued that these areas "had the potential to provide adequate space and habitat to maintain the grizzly bear as a viable and self-sustaining species." But it also acknowledged the risks and uncertainties facing the bears, and it pledged to assess other areas in their historical range.

This process was expected to take five years. Twenty-eight years later, in 2019, the FWS settled a federal lawsuit in which it agreed to finally conduct this long-delayed analysis. It built a simple model based mainly on secure habitat, and then applied it to both the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and the Sierra Nevada of California. Other potential recovery areas — such as the North Rim of the Grand Canyon in Arizona, the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico, and the Northwest Forest of Northern California — were, for unexplained reasons, not included.

The current grizzly bear recovery zones with the proposed boundaries.

The model did its job. According to the FWS, neither the San Juans nor the Sierra Nevada contained enough secure habitat to support a viable grizzly population. Instead of subjecting the study to peer review, the FWS published it in an appendix on page 286 of a species status report. Having pioneered the idea of secure habitat, David Mattson now set out to explain why the FWS was abusing it. In his view, the service's models focused on artificially small areas, failed to consider several key factors described in the scientific literature, and neglected to conduct essential supporting analyses to explain its conclusions.

The FWS had dragged its heels for almost three decades, and then, after pledging in court to conduct a good-faith analysis, produced a study that seemed designed to reach a predetermined result: The only places capable of supporting grizzlies were the places where the FWS was already trying to recover them. When Mattson and his colleague Troy Merrill ran a more detailed model for the southwestern states, they found that Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah contained seven potential recovery areas with more than 45,000 square kilometers of suitable habitat that could probably support more than 1,000 bears.

For more than a century, the prevailing narrative in California has been that the grizzly's extinction there was inevitable and its recovery is impossible. But Mattson's results for the southwest, combined with California's unique geography, cast doubt on this story.

California is home to nearly 40 million people, and it has more miles of roads than any state except Texas. But its population is extraordinarily concentrated. California is the most urban state, with 95% of its residents packed into cities and 75% living on only around 2% of its land area. Much of California has a human population density lower than that of the Northern Rockies. Unlike in the Northern Rockies, the majority of California's farms are concentrated in broad valleys dozens of miles from core wilderness habitats.

Kings Canyon National Park in California has been identified as one of the locations where grizzlies could thrive.

Outside urban and agricultural areas, California has more protected land than any state except Alaska, including the largest areas of potential grizzly habitat outside the six current recovery zones. Some of these protected areas are in desert ecosystems not suitable for grizzly bears, but others are in mountain ecosystems with potential grizzly habitat.

California's national parks and wilderness areas sometimes strain under heavy visitation, but the numbers paint a complex picture. Consider the southern High Sierra. In 2024, Sequoia Kings Canyon National Park, which is around 865,000 acres and 97% wilderness, topped 2 million visitors for the first time, whereas Yellowstone, which is around 2.2 million acres and 90% wilderness, received almost 5 million visitors, meaning that both parks had about 2.3 visitors per acre. Yellowstone has more than double the total land area in wilderness, but both parks border large U.S. Forest Service wilderness areas and other public lands, and the High Sierra has fewer roads cutting across its protected areas.

In 2024, I coauthored a study, almost eight years in the making, looking at potential grizzly habitat in California. This project, led by Alex McInturff from the University of Washington, ran four computer models, and then compared them to assess the results each produced. One of these models focused on historical sightings of grizzlies in California, two used approaches developed in other regions where brown bears currently live, and one looked at the habitat use preferences of one of California's other large carnivores, the puma.

The Grizzly Bear Recovery Program was created in the 1970s to restore populations to self-sustaining levels.

Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. None of them fully account for the distribution or abundance of food on the landscape or for possible conflicts with people. Together, however, they provide a first assessment of the amount, quality, and locations of potential grizzly habitats. Amazingly, about a third of California appeared as suitable habitat in all four models.

The biggest areas of high-quality habitat were in the southern Sierra Nevada, around Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, where some of the last California grizzly sightings occurred in the 1920s. The Northwest Forest, along the Pacific Coast near the Oregon border, also scored highly owing to its low human population density and rich forest habitats. The Transverse Ranges, in the state's southwestern corner, scored highly because of their rich chaparral habitats and density of historical sightings, but ranked somewhat lower than the other two because more people live, work, and grow crops, including extensive vineyards and avocado orchards, around its borders.

These results made intuitive sense, given the state's robust historical grizzly population, large areas of protected habitat, and healthy black bear populations. But they represented a departure from the conventional wisdom that dominated the circular logic of most habitat models. For the first time, it was clear how much potential habitat could be available in California for a grizzly recovery. But our approach still clung to the conservative assumption that the grizzly is a wilderness species. We had shown, with some important caveats, that California probably had enough wilderness to support one or more viable grizzly populations.

What we hadn't shown was whether Californians were willing to coexist with grizzlies that might, someday, wander outside the state's wilderness boundaries.

From the book START WITH A BEAR: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet, by Peter S. Alagona. Copyright © 2026 by Peter S. Alagona. Published by HarperOne, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Excerpted by permission.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

A century ago, prevailing wisdom cast large carnivores as adversaries—pests and threats to be removed for human safety and prosperity. In North America, among the most targeted of these animals were brown bears, or grizzlies, whose population decimation has made them emblematic of this fear-driven approach to wildlife management.

In California, where they once roamed the land in the tens of thousands, grizzlys have not been seen in more than 100 years. Modern conservation has evolved, yet it often remains rooted in a separation from nature, a systemic opposition that keeps the wild at arm's length.

In Start with a Bear, historian, ecologist, and bear expert Peter Alagona suggests we must reimagine the very heart of conservation, inviting a new framework for sustainable, reciprocal relations with the wild creatures that remain.

Peter S. Alagona is an environmental historian, conservation scientist, and nature-culture geographer. His work explores what happens when people share space and resources (their habitats) with other species: how we interact with non-human creatures, how we make sense of these interactions, why we fight so much about them, what we can learn from them, and how we might use these lessons to foster a more just, peaceful, humane, and sustainable society. He is a professor of environmental studies at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is the author of "After the Grizzly" and "The Accidental Ecosystem."

#6508. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.

#6505. A single drop of coolant could change how data centers cool their chips

Low-cost water handles steady heat and one costly coolant drop boils on the spikes, a data center cooling idea tested on a chip at Waterloo.

Cooling an overheating computer chip sounds like a job for more cold liquid. In a lab test, a single drop of coolant cooled a simulated chip’s hottest spot faster than a bath of the same coolant.

Engineers placed the drop, just over a quarter of an inch across, on a heated sapphire square submerged in water.

The drop boiled, and within 15 seconds the center of the hot spot had cooled by about 31°F (17°C).

The idea is to spend expensive coolant only where and when a chip needs it, and let low-cost water do the rest.

Sushanta Mitra, a professor of mechanical and mechatronics engineering at the University of Waterloo in Canada, led the work with postdoctoral researcher Tian-Yu Zhang and doctoral student Arnav Banerjee.

The test ran on a heated square of sapphire standing in for a chip, not on a working processor.

“It’s a division of labor,” said Mitra. “Water is excellent at handling steady, everyday heat and the drops take care of sudden spikes.”

Operators of data centers increasingly cool their servers by submerging the electronics in a liquid that doesn’t conduct electricity.

The trouble is that chips don’t heat evenly. AI workloads have pushed data centers toward denser processors that draw more power.

A processor core can run far hotter than the rest of the chip for a few seconds at a time. Such bursts make chips slow down and age faster, and a liquid that simply surrounds the chip responds slowly.

Coolants that boil pull heat away faster, but they’re costly, and boiling is hard to start at exactly the right spot.

Purified water moves heat better than the standard fluids, and with the electronics insulated it can serve as a coolant itself. In still water, though, the currents that carry heat away from a sudden hot spot can be slow to start.

The sapphire square measured 1.2 inches (30 millimeters) on each side and was thinner than a dime. An electric current heated a coating on its surface.

The chip sat under about 1 fluid ounce (30 milliliters) of purified water, less than half an inch deep.

The team squeezed a drop of Novec-7100, an electronics coolant that boils at about 142°F (61°C), onto the chip through a needle. The coolant is heavier than water and barely dissolves in it, so the drop stayed on the chip.

Then they switched on the power. The highest of three settings was about 86 watts, roughly a bright old-style light bulb’s heat packed into an area the size of a postage stamp.

An infrared camera under the chip recorded its temperature 30 times a second, and a high-speed camera filmed the bubbles. Each test ran three times.

For comparison, the team also ran the chip in a tank of pure coolant and in water alone.

At the highest heat setting, the drop made the difference.

Once the chip’s surface passed the coolant’s boiling point, bubbles formed inside the drop while the water around it stayed liquid. Within 15 seconds, the center of the hot spot was some 31°F (17°C) cooler.

A chip in a tank of pure coolant reached a similar peak temperature, but cooled far more slowly afterward. In water alone, the chip kept getting hotter.

“Boiling soaks up a lot of heat and the rising bubbles stir the surrounding water so it carries heat away faster,” said Mitra, who is also executive director of the Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology.

“We get the punch of boiling, but only where and when it’s needed.”

The chip surface around the drop also ran cooler than it did in water alone, so the drop was helping beyond the patch it covered.

The boiling drop had limits. At the lowest heat setting, water alone kept the chip coolest early on. And until the drop had boiled away, its own footprint ran up to 29°F (16°C) hotter than the surface around it.

Mitra’s lab specializes in wrapping one liquid in a thin skin of another, and the team tried it on the coolant drops.

The team floated a small ring from a plumbing supplier on the water, poured a thin layer of silicone oil inside it, and let coolant drip through the oil. Each drop picked up a silicone skin as it sank to the chip.

The silicone skin changed the boiling. At the middle heat setting, a plain silicone skin delayed boiling by about 1.5 seconds and let the hot spot climb about 14°F (8°C) higher first.

When boiling did start, it happened all at once, as one large bubble, and that drop cooled the chip faster than any other.

Mixing tiny particles of a heat-conducting ceramic, aluminum nitride, into the oil did the opposite. The particles gave bubbles places to start, so many small bubbles formed instead of one big one.

At the highest heat, those skins cut the peak hot-spot temperature by about 18°F (10°C).

Skins have a cost, though. Leftover oil on the chip surface slowed cooling later on, so the wrapped drops did worse than bare ones over a longer period.

Everything so far happened in still water on a heated square of sapphire, not on a processor in a working server.

Real cooling systems usually pump their liquid, and the authors wrote that boiling in flowing water may behave quite differently and needs its own tests.

High-heat runs also varied noticeably from one repeat to the next, though the overall pattern held each time.

Mitra’s team described two ways the idea could work. Sensors could detect a hot spot and deliver a drop to it, or wrapped drops could circulate in the water and boil wherever they land on something hot enough.

Next on the authors’ list are shell liquids that leave less residue, ways to wrap drops inside flowing coolant, and tests under realistic operating conditions.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Colloid and Interface Science.

#6503. What a city’s sewage can reveal about the health of the people upstream

Eight Ohio cities' sewage carried gut bacteria whose mix lined up with local obesity, blood pressure, and stroke rates, a pilot study finds.

During the pandemic, health departments learned to read a city’s sewage for the virus behind COVID-19.

The same water carries something else from every household that flushes into it: the bacteria living in people’s guts.

In eight Ohio cities, the mix of those gut bacteria in the sewage lined up with how the cities scored on chronic disease.

Cities with more of one group of bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide had higher rates of obesity, high blood pressure, stroke, and several other conditions.

The study rests on 27 samples collected over seven weeks in May and June 2022, and the authors wrote that the links do not show cause.

What they show is that a sample from a treatment plant can carry a readable signal about the health of the people upstream.

Emma Lancaster, then a doctoral student in the College of Public Health at Ohio State University, led the study with Jiyoung Lee, professor and chair of environmental health sciences.

Lancaster is now an environmental health consultant in Boston.

“During the pandemic, the world learned how to use wastewater to track infectious disease. We asked, what else can it tell us?” Lancaster said.

Sewage arriving at a treatment plant is a blend of everything a community has flushed.

One earlier study the authors cite found up to 97% of the microbes in human stool in untreated sewage.

So the water is a pooled sample of a whole population’s gut bacteria, collected without asking anyone to take a test.

Earlier sewage studies elsewhere had tied a community’s bacterial profile to its rates of obesity, high blood pressure, and smoking.

The Ohio team set out to build full gut bacteria profiles for a set of cities and test them against a wide range of health and social measures.

The team collected a liter of untreated wastewater from each of nine treatment plants, on three days in May and June 2022. Two of the plants serve Columbus, the state capital.

The rest serve smaller cities in central and southeastern Ohio: Zanesville, Marysville, Newark, Lancaster, Athens, Circleville, and Marietta.

Together the plants handle sewage from more than 1.3 million people.

The smallest serves about 15,000 and the largest nearly 548,000. So the cities range from small towns to a major metro area.

Four of the cities count as rural under the federal definition the team used, with fewer than 50,000 residents. The other four are urban.

Each sample was processed the same day. The team sequenced a marker gene to identify the bacteria present. Then they kept only those known to live in the human gut, about 37% of what they read.

For the health side, they pulled public estimates for the census tracts inside each plant’s service area, 329 tracts in all.

The CDC’s PLACES database supplied rates of 23 health conditions and behaviors.

The agency’s Social Vulnerability Index supplied the social and economic measures, such as poverty and unemployment.

Each city’s sewage had its own bacterial profile, and the profiles differed enough that the cities could be told apart.

Several of those differences lined up with health. Cities where smoking was more common had more of one large group of bacteria, the Firmicutes.

Cities with less physical activity had more of two genera, Desulfovibrio and Tolumonas.

Desulfovibrio, a genus of bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide, appeared again and again. Its abundance was associated with eight health measures.

They were high blood pressure, obesity, stroke, mobility disability, chronic kidney disease, coronary heart disease, chronic lung disease, and cancers other than skin cancer.

Studies of patients have found more Desulfovibrio in people with colorectal, stomach, and breast cancers than in healthy people, the authors wrote.

Researchers suspect its hydrogen sulfide may damage cells.

Asthma ran the other way. Cities with more asthma had a less even mix of gut bacteria and less of a genus called Akkermansia, which is widely treated as a marker of a healthy gut.

Social conditions showed up too. Cities with more unemployment had less diverse gut bacteria overall and more Firmicutes.

The four rural cities carried more Desulfovibrio, more Akkermansia, and more of a major group called Bacteroidota than the urban ones.

They also generally had higher rates of the chronic conditions in the dataset.

“In many cases, poor health outcomes are worse in rural areas and to see these distinct indicators of poorer gut microbiome health in these rural areas offers us clues to some of what is driving that,” Lancaster said.

Marysville, an urban city, sat at the healthy end of nearly every measure, with the lowest rates of smoking, depression, unemployment, and poverty among the eight.

“Wastewater offers a unique way to understand the health of whole communities, not just the people who show up in clinics,” Lee said.

Eight cities give eight data points. The authors wrote that their results should be read as exploratory, not as reliable estimates for any one city.

Columbus alone accounts for most of the 1.3 million people, which could tilt comparisons.

The health figures are also modeled estimates for census tracts, not counts of diagnosed patients. And the samples cover seven weeks of one year.

A deeper problem is in the pipes. Desulfovibrio and Acetobacterium live in sewers as well as in guts, and their numbers in wastewater can rise or fall with how long sewage stays in a pipe.

The authors wrote that future studies should record sewer conditions to separate the human signal from the plumbing.

A larger study could test whether the same patterns hold across more cities and over longer periods while accounting for diet, access to health care, and sewer conditions.

Wastewater already tracks viruses such as those behind COVID, flu, and mpox, Lee said.

Tracking a community’s gut bacteria the same way, she said, could eventually show whether a nutrition program is improving its gut health.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research.

#6502. Dragonfly wings inspired a new way to build materials that can take a hit

Engineers took cues from dragonfly wings to 3D-print materials that spread damage and absorb energy when compressed.

A neat grid or honeycomb looks like the smartest way to build something light and strong, and engineers have borrowed both for decades. Squeeze a printed grid hard enough, though, and it fails the way a stack of cans does.

One row buckles, then the next, in a band that runs across the whole piece.

A leaf’s veins, a dragonfly’s wing and a spider’s web are built the opposite way, from struts of wildly different sizes tangled together.

Materials printed on that plan spread the damage out instead of concentrating it. They also absorbed as much energy as the tidy lattices, or more.

Engineers at MIT and network scientists at Northeastern University’s Network Science Institute designed the new materials, which they call scale-rich metamaterials.

So far the team has tested them as flat, credit-card-sized polymer plates in a lab, not as helmets or packaging.

“This is a completely new way of thinking for metamaterials,” said study author Carlos Portela, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT.

Metamaterials get their properties from their internal architecture rather than their chemistry. Engineers usually design one small building block, a unit cell, and repeat it over and over.

So every strut inside is about the same length and thickness.

Albert-László Barabási, a physicist at Northeastern, has spent his career mapping networks from the internet to the brain. Those networks don’t look like a grid at all.

The veins in a dragonfly’s wing run from about four thousandths of an inch (0.1 millimeters) to about two inches (50 millimeters) long.

Leaf veins and spider silk span a range at least as wide, and the struts inside bone vary tenfold in thickness.

Barabási asked whether that spread of sizes could be built into a solid material on purpose. He took the question to Portela’s lab, with a mathematician at Utrecht University in the Netherlands joining the team.

The team’s recipe is short. A computer picks a random point inside a square and draws a straight beam through it at a random angle, until the beam hits the edge.

The computer picks another point and draws another beam, which stops when it meets the first.

Each new beam is thinner than the last, by a rate the designer sets. Only two settings matter: how thick the first beam is and how fast the thickness shrinks.

The program repeats the step hundreds of times, so the last beams are short and fine while the first few stay long and thick.

The finished design has no typical strut. Lengths, thicknesses and the number of crossings per beam all run across orders of magnitude inside one sample, the same pattern network scientists find in road maps and food webs.

Changing those two settings also changes how stiff the material is in different directions. Across 2,600 computer-generated designs, the directional stiffness varied 24-fold.

That is far more range than a square grid, a honeycomb or a random foam-like Voronoi pattern can offer.

The researchers 3D-printed the designs in a stiff polymer. Each sample was a few inches across, with beams from a few thousandths of an inch up to an inch or so long.

Then they squeezed the samples in a press, alongside square, honeycomb and Voronoi samples of the same density, about 42% solid, three of each.

The square grid buckled first in a single row, and the collapse spread sideways across the whole sample before the next row went. The honeycomb formed wide crushed bands.

Even the random Voronoi foam compacted from the bottom up while its top stayed untouched.

The scale-rich samples didn’t do that. Their stress rose smoothly as the press pushed down, with no sudden drops, and the crushing stayed spread across the whole piece.

The team scored that spread on a scale where zero means perfectly even deformation and one means all the damage in one spot.

The new samples stayed at or below 0.2 even after being compressed by 25% of their original height.

The energy they soaked up before packing down matched or beat the three conventional designs.

“Because there is such a richness of length scales in these networked materials, if one part fails, there is a strong web of structures around it that keeps the entire material from failing catastrophically,” Portela said.

“It’s more efficient at distributing damage and absorbing energy.”

For a final test, the team borrowed from the thick, graded rind of a pomelo, denser toward the outside.

They generated a network whose beams crowded the edges and steered load around a disc of clear acrylic embedded in the middle.

Under compression, the acrylic disc inside a square or honeycomb lattice showed bands of stress under polarized light. Inside the scale-rich network, the bands were far fewer.

Computer simulations put the stress on the disc at as little as about one-fifth of the stress in the conventional lattices.

The same two settings can also tune how fast vibrations travel through the material. The team used that to design a lens that focuses sound waves, so far only in simulation.

Everything the team crushed was a flat plate of one polymer, printed at a resolution of about four thousandths of an inch.

The authors showed on paper that the recipe extends to three dimensions, with plates or beams instead of lines. The stiffness trends carry over, but those 3D versions were simulated rather than squeezed.

The study didn’t test the materials as any product. Helmets, armor, packaging and crash parts are the uses the authors named, and each would need its own tests at full size.

The group has posted its generator code publicly. The authors wrote that a design needing only two inputs is well suited to AI-driven searches for structures with a target stiffness or energy absorption.

Future studies could run those searches, and print the 3D versions to see whether the even crushing holds in a solid block.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eagles can hunt exceptionally large prey, including a baboon that weighed nearly 60 pounds (26 kilograms), a new study finds.

Some human ancestors were smaller in size than modern-day humans and weighed around the same amount as the baboons. This raises the question of whether they also might have faced eagle attacks, the researchers said.

Until now, it was thought that eagles couldn't lift nonhuman primates weighing over 29 pounds (13 kg), the researchers reported.

Scientists made the finding while conducting research in the Sahara Desert in Chad. They found the remains of at least nine adult baboons that had been killed recently by eagles. The region is home to Verreaux's eagles (Aquila verreauxii), which hunt from cliff tops, sometimes in pairs, and have talons with a grip diameter of 16 inches (40 centimeters). Grip diameter is how far the eagle’s grip extends.

The scientists found deep talon marks on the baboons' bones. These marks suggest that the eagles hunted and killed the primates and brought parts of them back to their nests, the team noted in a paper published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

The photo on the left shows an eagle-baboon encounter, while another image (right) features a baboon skeleton with marks of eagle predation.

The baboons were sizable, with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kilograms). The largest of them weighed 58 pounds (26 kg), which is similar in size to some small hominins, a group that includes humans and our close relatives that arose after the split from chimpanzees and bonobos, the researchers noted. For instance, the Australopithecus afarensis individual known as Lucy weighed about 62 pounds (28 kilograms) when she was alive in what is now Ethiopia around 3.2 million years ago.

While eagles do sometimes scavenge carcasses, this doesn't seem to be the case with the baboons. The "severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip," the team wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

They noted that eight out of nine of the baboons in the study were male. This suggests that the baboons were hunted, since scavenged animal remains would not favor a particular sex. Why eagles hunted mainly male baboons is not clear, and the "male sex-bias in our sample is puzzling," the researchers noted. Male primates, such as monkeys, do sometimes defend against eagles by charging at them, the team added in a statement.

There is one known example of eagles hunting and killing a hominin. The "only confirmed case is Taung Child, an infant Australopithecus who we think was taken by a large eagle around 2.8 million years ago," study first author Catherine Hobaiter, a professor at the University of St. Andrews in the U.K. who has studied primates extensively, told Live Science in an email. The Taung Child weighed around 22 pounds (10 kg).

Hobaiter noted that "several of the australopithecine species who lived around 1 [million to] 3 million years ago would be in the same weight range as the adult male baboons in our study" and would have been vulnerable to eagle attacks. Other large predators, such as hyenas and crocodiles, also would have been a threat.

Nowadays, smaller primates, such as monkeys, defend against eagle attacks by traveling together.

"Modern primate species that are predated by eagles spend time in mixed species groups — for example foraging together," Hobaiter said. "That means extra competition for the food — but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost."

Hominins may have done something similar, with different hominin species traveling together to defend against eagle attacks, she noted.

An illustration of a Verreaux's eagle hunting an adult male baboon.

Robert Simmons, a researcher at the FitzPatrick Institute of African Ornithology at the University of Cape Town who wasn't involved with the study, called the findings "fascinating." Eagles "are opportunistic — an old male or a young male baboon dispersing to another troop found on its own can become prey to an opportunistic eagle, or a pair of eagles," Simmons said in an email. In a desert region, the lack of cover can leave baboons exposed.

This is "certainly a rare occurrence," he said. But in this dry desert environment, the prey available to the Verreaux's eagles is limited, which has forced them to take on larger, more dangerous prey than is typical for a 9-pound (4 kg) eagle, Simmons explained.

W. Scott McGraw, an anthropology professor at The Ohio State University who also wasn't involved with the study, said in an email that early "hominins may have been particularly attractive targets because of their relatively small body size," especially infants and juveniles.

"Given their limited physical defenses, early hominins — and, indeed, primates more generally — likely evolved a range of behavioral adaptations to reduce their vulnerability to raptors and other predators," McGraw said. These adaptations may have included living in groups, yelling out to warn others, and selecting habitats that could offer protection from attacks.

Jesús Bautista-Rodríguez, the coordinator of the Desert Golden Eagles Project who has conducted extensive research on eagles, said that the finds were interesting but was cautious about some of the conclusions.

"I am much more cautious, however, about interpreting the remains described in this paper as evidence that the eagles actively killed healthy adult male baboons weighing over 20 kg [44 pounds]," Bautista-Rodriguez told Live Science in an email. "In my opinion, it is quite possible that some, or even all, of these individuals were already dead, dying, severely weakened or otherwise unable to defend themselves when the eagles fed on them."

He also took issue with how the baboons died, saying that more fieldwork is needed to better understand how eagles came across the baboons.

“The punctures and extensive scratches observed on the skulls and scapulae are certainly interesting and compatible with eagle talons and feeding activity," Bautista-Rodriguez said. "Nevertheless, these marks do not necessarily demonstrate that the eagle was responsible for killing the animal. They could also have been produced during the handling, dismemberment and feeding of an individual that had already died."

Hobaiter, C., Akpona, T.J.D., Kopp, G.H., Dominy, N.J. (2026). Signs of eagle predation on a 22-kg adult primate. American Journal of Biological Anthropology. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.70377

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6500. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

This story was updated on November 13, 2026, to correct the spelling of Katy Croff Bell's name, and to correct the location of the corals mentioned in the story from the Indian to the Pacific Ocean.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6498. LSD changes the brain’s rhythm in a way earlier studies missed

Brain recordings from 17 volunteers show that LSD speeds up two brain rhythms even as it weakens them.

Brain recordings of people on psychedelics have told the same story for years: the brain’s steady electrical rhythms get weaker, as if the drug were turning the volume down.

A new analysis of recordings from 17 people given LSD finds that the volume isn’t the whole story. The drug also turns up the tempo.

LSD pushes two of the brain’s main rhythms to faster beats, and it makes the brain’s electrical activity more detailed and less predictable.

Venkatesh Subramani, a doctoral student at the Université de Montréal, led the analysis with his supervisor Karim Jerbi. Jerbi is a psychology professor there and a researcher at Mila, the Quebec artificial intelligence institute.

Co-authors included Nicolas Farrugia and Giulia Lioi of IMT Atlantique in France and Robin Carhart-Harris of the University of California, San Francisco.

“Imagine a radio station switching its broadcast frequency from 99.5 to 100.5 FM,” Jerbi said.

“If your radio stays tuned to 99.5, the signal may seem distorted or lost. In the same way, overlooking the shift to faster brain rhythms can lead us to misinterpret LSD’s effects on the brain.”

Groups of neurons firing together produce rhythms that a sensor outside the head can pick up. Researchers call them brain waves.

Alpha waves dominate when you rest with your eyes closed. Beta waves are faster and show up during concentration and decision-making.

Under psychedelics those waves look weaker, and the standard reading is that neurons are firing less in unison. Subramani’s team pointed out a catch.

If a rhythm speeds up, its peak can shift outside the frequency range researchers are measuring. That shift can make the wave look weaker even if its strength hasn’t changed.

So the team pulled the two possibilities apart. They first stripped out the brain’s rhythm-free background activity.

Then they located each person’s actual alpha and beta peaks under LSD and under placebo, and measured the power at those peaks.

The recordings were made at Imperial College London by Carhart-Harris’s group. Seventeen healthy volunteers came in twice, two weeks apart.

In one session, they received an intravenous injection of 75 micrograms of LSD, roughly the weight of a grain of salt. In the other they received a saline placebo, without being told which was which.

About four hours after the injection, each person lay in a magnetoencephalography scanner. It records the faint magnetic fields that neurons produce, with timing down to the millisecond.

They rested with their eyes closed for seven minutes, and in a separate seven-minute block they listened to ambient music.

The Montreal team reanalyzed those recordings with newer signal-processing tools and a machine-learning model trained to tell the LSD sessions from the placebo sessions.

Under LSD, alpha waves ran about 2 cycles per second faster than on placebo, and beta waves about 5 cycles per second faster, across large areas of the cortex. The waves did also weaken.

Once the speed-up was accounted for, that weakening held up as real rather than an artifact of looking in the wrong place.

The two effects didn’t fully overlap. The weakening was strongest in regions that handle hearing, language, and emotion.

The speed-up followed its own map, and the regions that weakened most tended to speed up least.

Anesthetics do the opposite to the alpha rhythm, slowing it down as the cortex becomes less excitable. The authors read the faster alpha under LSD as a sign of a more excitable cortex.

They also noted that psilocybin and DMT haven’t been shown to shift the peaks this way, so the speed-up may be a signature specific to LSD.

A fractal is a shape that repeats itself in its own parts, the way each floret of a Romanesco broccoli is a smaller broccoli.

The team measured how fractal the brain signal was over time, and how varied its patterns were. Both rose under LSD.

The increases were largest in areas tied to vision, hearing, memory, and mental imagery, and smallest in the motor cortex.

That split fits a familiar feature of the drug. Perception and inner experience change a great deal, while people can still move normally.

People on LSD often report seeing repeating geometric patterns with their eyes closed. The paper links the two only loosely.

“Our findings lend support to this intriguing hypothesis, but they do not yet confirm it,” Jerbi said. “We measure the fractal structure of brain signals over time, not the fractal structure of the images people perceive.”

Given only the shift in peak frequencies, the machine-learning model identified the LSD session more than 82% of the time.

Models trained on the fractal and complexity measures did almost as well. The brain regions the models relied on matched the ones the conventional statistics had flagged.

“Our machine-learning algorithm can distinguish brain states under LSD from those under placebo using brain signals alone,” Subramani said.

“By examining the clues it relies on, we can identify LSD’s signatures in brain activity.”

Music, which is routinely played during psychedelic therapy, didn’t amplify any of these effects. If anything the trend ran the other way, with slightly smaller brain changes during the music block.

That difference didn’t survive the statistical correction, and the authors called it exploratory.

Seventeen people is a small group, and everyone received a single dose while healthy, so the study says nothing about whether any of this helps patients.

The volunteers rated their experience at the peak of the drug’s effect, while the scanner ran about two and a half hours later.

The authors wrote that this gap may be why brain changes and reported experiences lined up only loosely.

The recordings also included no direct measure of muscle activity, which can contaminate the fastest brain signals. So the authors treated their high-frequency results with extra caution.

The next question is whether the speed-up really belongs to LSD alone.

Subramani and his colleagues are now running the same analysis on recordings taken under psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and under DMT.

The aim is to see whether the three drugs produce the same signatures in the brain or different ones.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

#6497. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#6496. Wind turbines may have killed nearly 19 million bats in the U.S. since 1981

A new study draws on decades of wind farm surveys to estimate how many bats turbines killed across the lower 48 states from 1981 to 2024.

The bats that die under wind turbines are picked up one carcass at a time, by crews walking the ground under each tower.

For decades, those site-by-site counts were the main tally anyone had.

Combining those counts with a statistical model, researchers estimated that wind turbines killed about 18.7 million bats in the lower 48 states from 1981 through the end of the study period.

Since 2021, the toll has run above 1.5 million a year. That is a scale the authors wrote may rival the fungal disease that has devastated cave-hibernating bats.

Charles Labuzzetta of the U.S. Geological Survey‘s Fort Collins Science Center led the analysis with colleagues at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Laboratory of the Rockies.

The figures are model estimates with wide ranges, built from monitoring that was never designed to be added up, and the relationships they found are correlations, not proven causes.

In an interview with Earth.com, Labuzzetta said the data behind the study were richer than their patchy origins suggest.

“We found that there could still be a lot to learn from the rich monitoring data that has been collected since the late 1990s and continues to be collected,” he noted.

The team pulled together 499 monitoring reports from 277 wind facilities in the lower 48 states, filed with the Fish and Wildlife Service since the late 1990s.

Each report counted the carcasses found under turbines and estimated how many were missed. But the searches differed in length, area and method, and many reports are confidential.

A statistical model pooled them, corrected for what the searchers could not see, and projected fatalities back to 1981.

The median came out at 18,696,140 bats across ten species, with a plausible range of about 13.3 million to 25.7 million.

That is the estimate for the lower 48 states that the compliance reports could never produce on their own.

Four species account for nearly all of it. The authors estimate about 6.7 million hoary bats, 5.8 million eastern red bats, 3.4 million silver-haired bats and 1.5 million big brown bats.

On average, a turbine killed close to six hoary bats a year. At the other end, the rare Indiana bat accounted for about 6,000 deaths over the whole period.

The last national figures date from 2013, and they put the toll in the hundreds of thousands a year.

Those estimates leaned on a single rule of thumb, about 1.7 hoary bats per megawatt of capacity.

A projection built on it assumed roughly 113,000 hoary bat deaths in 2012, and the new model estimates about 268,000 for that year. The old figure was less than half the new one.

The gap matters because of what the old projection, built on expert judgment, already said.

Run on the lower numbers, it warned that hoary bats could lose 50% to 90% of their population within 50 years. Eastern red bats have been dying faster still, more than 500,000 a year since 2021.

Rated capacity, the usual yardstick, turned out to be a poor predictor of deaths. The area swept by the blades was a better predictor.

On most turbines built since 2020 that is 2.5 to 5 acres (10,000 to 20,000 square meters).

Researchers estimated more deaths among several bat species at turbines whose blades swept a larger area or passed closer to the ground.

For all ten species, estimated deaths were higher at wind farms closer to rivers. The study couldn’t determine whether being near a river was itself responsible for the higher toll.

Labuzzetta told Earth.com those patterns point to siting and design as levers, but not to a single fix.

“There is still a great deal to learn about what strategies may be optimal and could provide the greatest conservation management return on investment for individual species and across all species,” he said.

White-nose syndrome, a fungal disease first seen in 2006, has cut some cave-hibernating species by more than 90%.

The authors compared their total with one rough estimate of the disease’s losses and found the two comparable in size.

The two threats mostly hit different bats. The disease kills bats that hibernate in caves, while turbines mostly kill the migratory tree-roosting species.

Across North American bats as a whole, the authors wrote, the two may compound.

Whether 18.7 million deaths translate into shrinking populations is the question the study can’t answer.

Data on how many hoary or eastern red bats exist, how long they live and how fast they breed are largely unavailable, the authors wrote. So the same number of deaths could mean a crisis or a dent.

“Our research alone cannot answer whether fatalities from wind energy are leading to similar population-level declines for migratory tree-roosting bat species,” Labuzzetta said.

Population trends from the North American Bat Monitoring Program could begin to fill that gap.

The authors also called for monitoring at wind farms to be collected and shared in a form that can be pooled.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
